sources.news_title: Did Trump Learn Anything From the Midterms? We Already Have Our Answer.
sources.text:
Hour 3 of the Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show is dominated by breaking political news, extensive analysis of White House personnel changes, the future of the Trump administration after the 2026 midterm elections, and early speculation surrounding the 2028 Republican presidential race. The hour begins with the major announcement that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House Chief of Staff, prompting Clay and Buck to examine what the move signals about President Donald Trump’s priorities moving forward. The hosts praise Miller as one of Trump's closest and most influential advisers, arguing that his promotion reflects a renewed emphasis on immigration enforcement, border security, deportation policy, and America First governance. They contend that elevating Miller demonstrates that the administration intends to maintain a hardline stance on illegal immigration and border control despite political setbacks in the midterm elections.
A significant portion of Hour 3 focuses on interpreting what Susie Wiles's departure means for the future of the Republican Party and the emerging battle for leadership after President Trump leaves office. Clay and Buck explore the possibility that Wiles' move from the White House into Trump's political operation positions her to become a major kingmaker ahead of the 2028 election cycle. The hosts speculate about which Republican candidate may ultimately inherit the Trump political infrastructure, donor network, fundraising apparatus, and campaign machinery. Much of the discussion centers on whether Senator Marco Rubio or Vice President JD Vance emerges as the favorite to carry the MAGA movement into the next presidential contest. They repeatedly emphasize that the race for 2028 has effectively begun immediately following the 2026 midterm results and that political maneuvering is already underway behind the scenes.
The hosts also analyze the internal fallout from Republican losses in the 2026 midterm elections. They argue that someone inside the administration was likely going to bear responsibility for the disappointing results and debate whether Wiles became the political casualty of broader dissatisfaction within Trump's inner circle. Clay and Buck discuss reports that tension existed among senior administration officials over strategy, messaging, and policy decisions, particularly regarding foreign policy and the administration's handling of Iran. They suggest that Wiles' departure reflects larger efforts by President Trump to reorganize his team and position the White House for the final two years of his presidency while preparing for the next generation of Republican leadership.
Foreign policy, national security, and administration infighting emerge as another major theme of the hour. The hosts examine reports involving Pete Hegseth and ongoing debate over the administration's Iran policy. They discuss whether policy disagreements and political consequences stemming from military actions against Iran contributed to recent personnel changes and power struggles within the administration. Clay and Buck analyze public statements from administration figures and speculate about which officials gained influence in the aftermath of the midterm losses. The conversation frequently returns to the question of how Trump intends to balance foreign policy priorities, national security concerns, and domestic political pressures during the remainder of his term.
A substantial segment is devoted to potential 2028 Republican contenders. The hosts compare the positioning of Marco Rubio, JD Vance, and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, examining their strengths, weaknesses, and future strategic options. Rubio is discussed as a candidate who could potentially broaden Republican appeal among Hispanic voters while leveraging his extensive foreign policy experience and ties within the Trump coalition. Vance is analyzed as Trump's sitting vice president, though the hosts debate whether the burdens of that role could limit his ability to establish a distinct political identity. DeSantis is highlighted as someone benefiting from being outside the administration and therefore able to openly critique decisions and shape his own political profile heading toward 2028. The hosts repeatedly return to the idea that relationships among these figures, rather than direct confrontation, may ultimately determine how the Republican primary unfolds.
The discussion also examines broader questions about presidential succession, political ambition, and historical precedent. Clay and Buck review how vice presidents historically fare when attempting to succeed presidents from their own party and debate whether remaining in the administration helps or hurts future presidential prospects. They note the challenges associated with running for president while serving in a high-profile administration role and explore whether figures such as Rubio could eventually leave their current positions to build independent political brands before the next election cycle. The hosts argue that the Republican Party now faces a critical period of transition as it begins determining who will lead the movement after Trump.
Listener calls add further discussion about generational politics, younger voters, and demographic outreach. One caller argues that JD Vance may ultimately prioritize family life over another national campaign, while another cites growing enthusiasm among younger voters for Marco Rubio. Clay and Buck use these calls to discuss voter coalition building, particularly among Hispanic Americans and younger conservatives. They suggest that the Republican Party's future success may depend on expanding beyond its traditional base and identifying leaders capable of connecting with emerging demographic groups without alienating core supporters.

sources.news_title: Did Trump Learn Anything From the Midterms? We Already Have Our Answer.
sources.text:
This story is adapted from the Slatest newsletter. You can sign up here to get it in your inbox every day.
After suffering a historic rebuke in this week’s midterms, the infamously brash Donald Trump sounded almost chastened. “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them,” he said of Democrats in a subdued election-night phone call with the New York Times. “We’ll probably work something out.” Even as Trump emphasized his power to veto legislation, his postelection comments led some to imagine that a humbled dealmaker in chief might really be willing to play ball. “Donald Trump may be a bit crazy, but he is not stupid, and he is a good politician,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said on MSNBC, suggesting the president might even be open to signing a Medicare for All bill into law.
In the end, Trump’s conciliatory tone lasted less than three days. On Friday afternoon, the president announced that he was elevating Stephen Miller, an anti-immigrant hawk who has been with him since the 2016 campaign, to be his next White House chief of staff, describing Miller as “one of my most trusted advisors.” Democrats, including some who previously sounded hopeful about persuading Trump to back legislation that would lower costs for inflation-pinched Americans, reacted with fury. “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” wrote Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next House speaker. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”
It isn’t unusual for presidents to reshuffle the org chart after a midterm drubbing. But those personnel changes are usually a tacit admission that something has gone wrong, a public hitting of the reset button. After Republicans flipped the House in 2010, Barack Obama replaced Rahm Emanuel, his feisty chief of staff, with Bill Daley, a pragmatic centrist whom Obama hoped could help him work across the aisle. In the wake of a brutal loss, letting certain heads roll can look like a politically savvy sop to the will of the voters.
But Trump, who infamously tried to overturn his 2020 election defeat, has never cared much for the will of the voters. And promoting Miller, who is among the administration’s most despised figures, is the opposite of what most presidents would do after an overwhelming electoral beatdown. Even among Trump aides, Miller has an unusually long history of bigotry. In high school, he criticized administrators for allowing Spanish-language announcements and once reportedly jumped into a girls’ track race in an apparent attempt to prove the athletic superiority of men. In college, he wrote columns for Duke’s student newspaper that criticized feminism and argued that “Christianity is embedded in the very soul of our nation.” As an aide to an Alabama senator, Miller promoted white-supremacist talking points, including the racist “great replacement” conspiracy theory. After arriving at the White House, he zealously defended separating migrant families at the border. In the president’s second term, Miller helped architect Operation Metro Surge, the January immigration-enforcement blitz in Minneapolis that killed two American citizens whom Miller falsely branded domestic terrorists and assassins.
At first glance, doubling down on Miller now looks like a strange choice even for Trump. The president appears to be well aware of how extreme his adviser’s views are. As the Wall Street Journal reported this week in a midterms postmortem, Trump has privately admitted that Miller’s zeal for deportations had “gone too far.” The evidence suggests that backlash to those efforts helped sweep Republicans out of power across the country this week, particularly among Latino voters.
But promoting Miller starts to make more sense when you consider who Trump is at his core: a confrontational man who managed to get elected president twice in large part by stoking divisions over immigration. Ever in search of a scapegoat for his own failures, Trump has reportedly blamed Republicans’ hefty midterm losses on Susie Wiles, whom Miller is set to replace as chief of staff. And rather than confront the reality of defeat, Trump appears to be seeking succor among his core supporters. “Prominent MAGA figures I talked to this week cited Stephen Miller as their dream choice for chief of staff,” the Daily Mail reporter Charlie Spiering posted after the news broke. “This pick really re-energizes a gloomy base.” The president also prizes loyalty, and Miller spent the years between Trump’s terms laying the groundwork for a “spectacular migration crackdown.”
We’ve also lived through a version of this before. In 2018, after Democrats retook the House, Trump sounded similar notes of conciliation. “We have a lot of things in common on infrastructure,” he said the day after the election. “We want to do something on healthcare, they want to do something on healthcare, there are a lot of great things we could do together.” None of it ended up happening. Instead, the president soon found himself in a standoff with Democrats over his demand that a government funding bill include money for his southern border wall, an impasse that yielded what was then the longest government shutdown in U.S. history.
A repeat performance may already be in the offing. The federal government will run out of money next month, and elevating Miller isn’t the only sign that Trump plans to keep immigration at the forefront. “Deportations will continue,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin posted after Democrats won the House and Senate. Even Vice President J.D. Vance, who on Wednesday published a 600-word X post blaming the war in Iran for Republicans’ dismal midterm, showed little interest in finding common ground over immigration. “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance,” Vance wrote. “But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.” On Friday, Vance put out a statement congratulating Miller on his promotion.
Elevating Miller isn’t the only sign that Trump plans to spend the last two years of his second term the same way he spent the first two. Democrats won key races by casting the president as an out-of-touch billionaire more interested in beautifying Washington than in making groceries cheaper, but Trump is already hitting the gas on finishing his White House ballroom and erecting a triumphal arch near the Lincoln Memorial. After an election in which many voters rejected building data centers to power artificial intelligence, Trump reiterated in a Friday post on Truth Social that “only foolish leadership will say ‘NO’ to the riches they bring!” And even as key Trump allies seem to want the president to make Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth the fall guy for Iran, some reporters think replacing Wiles with Miller could save Hegseth’s job.
But the core issue of Miller’s promotion is immigration, the subject of the incoming chief of staff’s overriding obsession. For nearly two years now, this administration’s deportation policies have brought death, violence, and misery to communities across the country. With Miller at the helm, it would be a surprise if the next two years turn out much better.
On that cheery end-of-week note, let’s pivot to my colleagues’ suggestions about how to get your weekend off to a happier start:
Take stock of election week: It has been a truly wild week in politics, one that we’ll be making sense of for months and even years to come. Need some help? Tomorrow, the Surge—Slate’s weekly political analysis newsletter—will send out its postelection edition. We got an early look, and it’s a great one. You’ll want to sign up here.
A school staple gets revisited: Millions of students had to read the coming-of-age wilderness survival novel Hatchet in English class. It turns out that there’s a reason the book was inescapable for so many kids. Luke Winkie gets to the bottom of its unexpectedly controversial reputation.
A highly anticipated sequel falls flat: Romantasy fans have been waiting for more than five years for the latest installment in Sarah J. Maas’ A Court of Thorns and Roses series. Now that A Court of Splintered Harmony is finally here, it feels frustratingly incomplete. Nadira Goffe explains why some fans feel shortchanged by this sequel.
A quintessential American author gets his due: There are countless American writers who have shaped the country’s literary landscape, but one famous figure rarely gets mentioned in the conversation. Laura Miller makes the case that Edgar Allan Poe—whose work deliberately eschews many of the essential themes of American literature—is actually the most influential American writer of them all.
A time-traveling sequel arrives: The Time Traveler’s Wife was a blockbuster hit in 2003. Now, more than 20 years later, a sequel has arrived. Ironically, the inventive time-travel tale feels of a totally different era from its predecessor. Rebecca Onion assesses some of the book’s mind-bending challenges for readers.
Congratulations on making it to Friday! You’ve earned a break from the news, but I promise we’ll be back in your inbox on Monday with more. Enjoy the weekend.

sources.news_title: Trump’s surprising move after midterm shellacking
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter.
WATCH THE VIDEO ABOVE: Trump appoints Stephen Miller as new chief of staff
Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today
He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.
The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday’s midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target.
Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president’s executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told the Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation.
Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement.
“I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Miller is tied to immigration policies that voters said went too far
During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoting unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.
He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program.
He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.
He joined Trump on Friday for his trip to Florida, and the president noted to reporters that “Stephen has been with me from the beginning.
“He gets it; very good politically,” Trump said as he departed the White House.
“He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”
But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely associated with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election.
The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.
“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Californian Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee.
“Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”
In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”
Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign
Trump on Friday praised Wiles, the veteran Florida operative who joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid, as having done a “very good job, great job.”
But he added: “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves”.
Wiles, 69, is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
She has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.”
Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
Wiles stuck with the job even after her breast cancer diagnosis. Deep into the midterm campaign, six months after having revealed her diagnosis, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear.
In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer.
Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.
Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign.
She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.
Wiles once said Trump had ‘an alcoholic’s personality’
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff.
She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

sources.news_title: Donald Trump should resign. Congress should demand it
sources.text:
Donald Trump should resign. Congress should demand it
Promoting Stephen Miller after the miderms proves he should go now.
I do not think the president actually believed it Thursday when he said that any attempt to impeach and remove him “would destroy the Democrat Party.” He added that it would be “impeachment for no reason, what for having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in its history.” That claim was barely plausible before Tuesday. The midterms, however, were a generational wipeout. They were bigger than any wave election going back half a century. The result is that Donald Trump’s name is mud. While his delusions know no bounds, I don’t think even an old scammer like him believes it.
The damage is deeper than Trump cares to know. The Democrats reversed the decade and a half that began with the 2010 midterms. During that time, Republicans repeatedly routed Democrats for not only federal offices, but state and local offices, down to the level of town comptroller, boards of education and county commissioner. There’s a legion of sheriffs that was swept into office by the white-power reaction to Barack Obama’s election. Tuesday’s midterms rolled back all that. The Democrats' numbers are now where they were in 2008.
“We really haven’t seen anything like this in 50 years,” Amy Walters, the editor-in-chief of the Cook Political Report, told New York magazine, noting that it took 15 years for the Democratic Party to come back from the “shellacking” of 2010. “We’re talking about the federal level, but it’s the state level as well. And so that is also a seismic change.”
This historic reversal should alarm Trump. His hold on the Republicans originated during the backlash against America's first Black president. That backlash was the context in which conservatism became white nationalism, or maga. (Remember that Trump was one of the original “birthers.") Tuesday’s elections restored the Democrats to the early years of Obama’s first term. That suggests that the backlash is now finally spent, which suggests that Trump is also finally spent. Exhaustion begets exhaustion, and while he may be acting like he’s untouchable, given the wholesale collapse of his coalition, Trump is very much touchable.
I’m sure there are some Senate Republicans who are still willing to defend the president, but at this point, it feels like the Democrats’ game to win or lose, not Trump’s. So the question is how to proceed, and one option seems obvious when you think about it: ask Trump to resign.
To be sure, Trump is a demented narcissist who has no future. In essence, he’s a suicide bomber. He would rather blow up the party than let any Republican think about succeeding him. But that’s all the more reason why his party might want his departure to be a consequence of choice rather than of impeachment. The Republicans would have to spend capital they don’t have defending him against Democratic aggression. That might please GOP voters still clinging to the glory days. But to spare themselves from going down with a sinking ship, the Republicans might prefer he leave on his own, “in service to the nation.”
I admit I don’t know what incentives they might offer. What I do know is things are not going to get better for them as long as Donald Trump is in the White House. His reaction to the midterms pretty much justified their outcome. While previous presidents acknowledged defeat, and their own role in it, Trump denied having anything to do with the wipeout and chose to spend Wednesday giving reporters a tour of a new ballroom construction site, as if he had not just seen Americans reject the open corruption that a new ballroom construction site represents. It was enough for a CNN talking head to wonder aloud if he were “dissociating.” “This is how he wants to spend his time in Washington and now, because he has only two years left, he thinks he can focus even more on some of these vanity projects.”
But the biggest reason the Republicans should be thinking about asking the president to resign came today when he replaced Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller. As the White House chief of staff, Wiles is chaos incarnate, but she is not directly responsible for dispatching a paramilitary police force to harass, terrorize and murder immigrants and citizens around the country. Stephen Miller is. Along with the economy, ICE is why Hispanic voters revolted against the Republicans. Sixty-eight percent of them disapprove of Trump’s deportation policies, per the Associated Press. They were key to flipping a Senate seat in Kansas. They were key to turning all of Texas blue. Trump should have fired Miller to show he learned a lesson. By elevating Miller, however, the president is telling the world, but especially his own party, that he is going to double down on the worst that the American people rejected.
Again, things are not going to get better. The Democrats should capitalize on that by asking Trump to resign. There is no downside to asking, no cost to them. All they need to do is point out how it would be better for everyone if this demented narcissist, who has no interest in being president, not to mention being commander-in-chief, would leave on his own. The American people have spoken. A new era has come. The old days are over. Yet he’s clearly not hearing the message. So it’s up to his party to step up and explain what’s happening. The Democrats can say Trump and the Republicans have a choice: the easy way or the hard way.
[Leave a tip in the tip jar! Say $10? THANKS!]
I don’t want to hear about the vice president. As I said before, no one likes JD Vance. He has humiliated himself so often, he can’t be trusted or taken seriously by anyone. But by asking Trump to resign, the Democrats can exploit his cynicism and ambition. He has already blamed Trump’s war against Iran for midterm losses. (And Trump agreed!) If there’s a chance for him to be president before the first ballot is cast in 2028, it’s possible he will take it. And if he does, that might hasten the unwinding of the Trump era even faster than it already is.
The Democrats have spent years on defense.
Here's a rare chance to go on offense at no cost.
Coda
As I was writing this piece, Stephen Miller got on the TV. After the midterms, he's no longer as scary as he was, but he's still pretty damn scary, as his boss, a demented narcissist, just gave him a promotion in the White House. Pay attention to Jake Tapper. The news anchor is a cynical opportunist. He knows which way the wind is blowing. It's not hard to imagine him, and others like him in the media, seeing Trump's resignation as bipartisan compromise.

Washington – U.S. President Donald Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress.
Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration.
A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party’s defeat in Tuesday’s midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

sources.text:
This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump doubles down on everything that lost him the midterms
Stephen Miller will be the new White House chief of staff, Trump said on Friday.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is doubling down after a midterm annihilation.
What happened? On Friday afternoon, Trump announced that longtime aide Stephen Miller would take over as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. In a post to Truth Social, Trump said that Miller would start on Monday, but the change appears to be effective more or less immediately — Wiles has already resigned.
Why the change? Trump was reportedly angry with Wiles over the GOP’s collapse in the midterm elections, which saw Democrats winning up and down the ballot even in traditionally deep-red parts of the country.
Trump, for his part, told reporters on Friday that Wiles had “done a very good job.” But, he added, “we gotta make moves. Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”
What should I know about Miller? Miller is currently the White House deputy chief of staff for policy, as well as homeland security adviser. More importantly, he’s the architect and engine of some of Trump’s most vicious immigration policies, including family separation (during the first Trump term) and ICE’s current campaign of indiscriminate, militarized immigration enforcement.
He’s also an ally of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has to be feeling a little bit better about his imperiled job (though it won’t keep Hegseth from facing impeachment in the near future).
What does this mean for the Trump presidency? More of the same, cranked up to 11. Miller is as hardline as they come, and he’s certain to push Trump to be even more aggressive on immigration and attempts to use the machinery of government to attack their shared political enemies.
It’s all going to be extraordinarily unpopular, if Tuesday’s midterm results are anything to go by — but with just over two years left in the White House, there’s little reason to believe that Miller and Trump won’t try to push the power of the presidency to its breaking point.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
Let’s end the week on a high note with this piece from my colleague Christian Paz, who writes that “the decency was the point” for voters and Democratic candidates alike in the 2026 midterms. You can read it here with a gift link.
If you’d prefer something even lighter to head into the weekend, I also recommend the Smithsonian’s cheetah cam. Enjoy, have a great weekend, and we’ll see you on Monday!

sources.news_title: Trump elevates hard-line immigration adviser Stephen Miller to chief of staff after GOP's midterm defeat
sources.text:
The Briefing:
- President Trump announced via Truth Social that Stephen Miller will become White House Chief of Staff on November 9, 2026, replacing Susie Wiles.
- Wiles — the first woman ever to hold the position and Trump's longest-serving chief of staff — submitted her resignation Thursday night, just days after the GOP's historic midterm collapse.
- Democrats swept both the House and Senate on Tuesday, flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts in the worst Republican showing in decades.
President Donald Trump moved decisively to put a new face atop his West Wing on Friday, announcing the departure of Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and naming her successor just days after the Republican Party absorbed one of the most punishing electoral defeats in a generation. Axios confirmed that Stephen Miller, the hard-line immigration strategist who has held Trump's ear for more than a decade, will officially take over the role on Monday, November 9.
The choice is a statement in itself. Rather than moderating course in the wake of a catastrophic midterm repudiation, Trump is elevating the man most identified with the administration's most aggressive policy impulses — an outcome that few Washington insiders found surprising, even as it unsettled many of them.
A Resignation Nobody Was Supposed to See Coming
As recently as October 16, Trump had publicly swatted away any suggestion that Wiles was headed for the exit. He praised her resilience — including her continued work through cancer treatment — and said she would stay as long as she wanted. Axios reported that Trump had even cleared a dedicated room inside the White House where Wiles could rest during the 12-hour days she worked while undergoing chemotherapy.
But behind those public endorsements, a quiet campaign to push her out had been gathering force. CNN reported that rivals had been forwarding Trump negative coverage tied to foreign consulting work conducted by members of Wiles' political circle, including longtime advisers James Blair and Chris LaCivita, as well as her daughter Katie Wiles.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation Thursday night, a person with knowledge of the conversation told the Associated Press, speaking anonymously to describe a private exchange. By Friday afternoon, she confirmed the departure herself in a post on X, writing that it marked her final day in the role.
The Midterm Factor
The timing of the announcement makes the connection to Tuesday's results impossible to separate. Democrats swept to control of both the House and Senate in a historic wave, according to CNBC, flipping at least seven Senate seats — including previously safe Republican strongholds in Texas, South Carolina and Kansas — and capturing more than two dozen House districts. Republicans failed to flip a single Democratic seat in return, a shutout that underscored the full breadth of the collapse.
Trump had been sounding out allies about a replacement even before election night, CNN reported, privately asking whether Miller was the right person for the job. After the results landed, the right flank of the MAGA movement moved quickly to assign blame. Former White House adviser Steve Bannon called publicly on The Hill for Wiles to be "removed immediately" over the GOP's losses.
Who Was Susie Wiles?
Wiles leaves Washington having accomplished something genuinely exceptional in Trump's orbit. As PBS NewsHour noted, she was both the first woman ever to serve as White House chief of staff and Trump's longest-serving in the position, outlasting all four people who held the role during his first term. Where the original administration was defined by constant internal warfare and upheaval, Wiles imposed a discipline on the second term that earned her a reputation as an indispensable stabilizing force.
She was widely regarded inside Washington as the most consequential figure in the administration outside the president himself — a manager whose grip on information flow and factional rivalries kept the second-term West Wing substantially quieter than the first. Trump himself had described her management style using the phrase "ice maiden." In her statement Friday, Wiles described the role as "the honor of a lifetime."
Stephen Miller: From Immigration Architect to West Wing Gatekeeper
Miller, 41, has been a central presence in Trump's political universe since joining his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter, having previously served as a senior aide and communications director for then-Senator Jeff Sessions. His fingerprints are on virtually every hard-line immigration measure the administration has pursued, from mass deportation operations to the systematic effort to restrict asylum rights at the southern border. As deputy chief of staff, he simultaneously held the title of Homeland Security Adviser, giving him sweeping policy reach across multiple agencies.
His elevation to the top staff role carries a clear ideological signal. CNN reported that the move indicates the president does not plan to fundamentally change his governing approach following the midterm losses. Former Trump deputy press secretary Sarah Matthews — who resigned from the administration after January 6th — had been unsparing in her assessment before the official announcement, telling MeidasTouch that Miller taking the chief of staff role would be "a terrifying prospect," the Daily Beast reported.
What This Shift Means for the Final Two Years
The practical consequences of the transition may be substantial. Where Wiles operated as a mediating presence — filtering impulses, managing competing factions and imposing structured process on a White House prone to chaos — Miller is a conviction-driven ideologue with a consistent track record of pushing the administration toward its most aggressive edges.
Internal administration documents reported publicly in June 2026 by Reason magazine revealed that White House Staff Secretary Will Scharf had authored confidential memos to Wiles cautioning against two of Miller's proposals: suspending the constitutional right of detained immigrants to challenge their confinement in court — known as habeas corpus — and invoking the Insurrection Act to deploy military force domestically. Those memos were directed at Wiles because she represented the principal institutional check on those impulses. With Miller now holding the chief of staff position, those guardrails become considerably harder to enforce.
Wiles will not vanish entirely from Trump's orbit, transitioning instead to the Trump Political Operation. But her departure removes the administration's most significant internal counterbalance. With no congressional majority to pass legislation, and the administration's most aggressive enforcer now sitting in the most powerful staff chair in the building, the final chapter of Trump's presidency may be defined less by lawmaking than by executive power pressed hard against its constitutional limits.

Critics of the administration were quick to denounce the appointment of Miller, who has a long documented history of promoting white nationalist literature and conspiracy theories.
“Stephen Miller is a vile, hate-filled extremist who has made cruelty his life’s work,” wrote the social media account of Democrats serving on the US House Committee on Homeland Security. “America just rejected the fear and bigotry he peddles and Trump handed him a promotion. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)—likely the chamber’s next speaker—described Miller as a “dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands.”
“His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor,” Jeffries added. “Fire him today.”
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is in line to be the next chair of the House Oversight Committee, issued a statement advising Miller to “lawyer up,” echoing his message to Trump earlier this week.
“Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional [US Immigration and Customs Enforcement] raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families,” Garcia said. “Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts.”
Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) said appointing Miller was “a giant middle finger to every single voter who came out to the polls and demanded a change from the corruption and cruelty of the last two years.”
Jayapal vowed that Democrats in Congress would deliver “real accountability for the corruption that Stephen Miller and Trump profited from.”
Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.) marveled that Trump elevated a hard-liner like Miller, even after his party suffered a historic defeat this week in the 2026 midterm elections.
“Tell me you learned nothing about why you had a devastating loss at the polls in November without telling me you don’t know why,” wrote Pocan. “Stephen Miller. The solution to nothing.”
Pocan’s remarks were echoed by Democratic Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who responded to news of Miller’s appointment by writing, “These losers learned nothing.”
Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), in a statement sent to independent journalist Marisa Kabas, warned Miller to not “get too comfortable with your new title.”
“Part of the benefits package for your promotion is accountability for all the pain you have caused,” Ramirez added.
Democrats weren’t the only ones panning the appointment of Miller, as some Republicans criticized the decision as well.
Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.), who earlier this week called for Miller’s firing, told Semafor reporter Nicholas Wu that making him White House chief of staff was a “horrible decision” by the president.
Outgoing Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told CNN’s Jake Tapper that picking Miller was “not a good choice” on Trump’s part.
“He’ll have an antagonistic relationship with many,” Bacon explained. “He did take the immigration issue for President Trump from a two-to-one favorable to a two-to-one unfavorable. He went from the Biden extreme to the other extreme. He cost us seats in Texas and Arizona by alienating many Hispanic voters who voted for Trump in 2024.”
Olivia Troye, former homeland security and counterterrorism adviser to Vice President Mike Pence, expressed disgust at Miller’s promotion.
“Stephen. Fucking. Miller,” she wrote. “What a dangerous joke. Except no one is laughing.”

“On the one hand, I think putting Miller in the driver’s seat puts all of us in genuine danger,” Bouie wrote. “On the other hand, if you want a path to 60-plus Senate seats in 2029, this is it.”

“If you were thinking: What could Trump do to push his approval rating down even further and open up the possibility of a 1964/1980/2008-style victory for Dems in 2028?” wrote Hayes. “The answer is: put Stephen Miller in charge of everything. And guess what?”

Trump Names Stephen Miller Chief of Staff After Midterms
sources.text:
President Trump has replaced Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with longtime adviser Stephen Miller after Republican midterm losses, moving to a sharper defense of his agenda against coming Democratic probes.
In a Friday Truth Social post from Washington, Trump said Miller, already deputy chief of staff and one of his most trusted advisers, will take the top staff job starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Wiles, who managed Trump’s successful 2024 campaign, will shift to the Trump Political Operation after 21 months in the West Wing.
“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote.
“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff, She has done a great job!” he added.
The change lands after Republicans suffered a landslide midterm defeat that flipped legislative power. A White House official framed the moment plainly: “There are still many who are gearing up for the challenge. It’s time to fight even harder.” Selection of Miller points to a more combative posture next year as Democrats gear up congressional investigations.
Wiles, 69, brought stability and cohesion to the West Wing during her 21-month run, the longest of any Trump chief of staff and the first by a woman. She was diagnosed with breast cancer while serving. A source close to her said she tendered her resignation the day before the announcement.
Fox News reported the decision as very amicable, with Wiles handing in her resignation Thursday night after the GOP midterm losses. She leaves with public praise from the president and no public feud.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” Wiles said. “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”
“More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will,” she continued.
Her move keeps a proven campaign operator inside the broader Trump political machinery rather than cutting her loose. That continuity matters after a midterm thrashing that already has staffers talking about further changes.
Miller, 41, has worked for Trump since the day he entered the White House in 2017. He served as a top speechwriter in the first term, later as homeland security adviser, and most recently as deputy chief of staff for policy. He has been a key conduit with federal agencies and a driving force behind the mass deportation campaign.
Just The News noted Miller’s reputation as an immigration and deportations hawk, with the shift coming amid calls for Wiles’s ouster after the midterms and uncertainty over any broader policy change. His second-term portfolio also included overseeing release of declassified UFO files.
At an Oct. 21 event in the East Room focused on anti-fraud efforts and cybercrime, Miller stood with the president and delivered a clear defense of the America First record.
“You’ve put the American people’s safety first,” Miller told Trump. “There’s a common theme in all of the challenges that you have systemically tackled and solved, whether it’s the trade deficit, where we were getting ripped off by foreign countries, whether it’s welfare fraud, where we’re getting ripped off by these refugees and foreign scammers, or cybercrime, where you have entire foreign economies that are propped up on stealing from American seniors.”
“What you’re saying is America is not a pile of treasure for other countries and other people and other scammers all around the world to loot for themselves. You’re protecting American wealth for American people and American families in a way no leader has ever done before,” he said.
That language tracks the same priorities, border security, fraud crackdowns, and putting citizens first, that defined the first stretch of the term. Miller’s wife, Katie Miller, served as an official in both Trump terms, a family tie that has drawn outside pressure in other contexts, including a cyberstalking case that reached federal charges.
The same midterm blowout that prompted the chief-of-staff change has put other names in play. Reporting flags potential further moves involving Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, over their roles connected to the Iran war, roles some link to the scale of the legislative reverse.
West Wing personnel fights are nothing new in this orbit. Separate episodes have shown how quickly internal reviews and external pressure can sideline officials, from FBI counterterrorism shifts tied to threat assessments to lawsuits by former agents over firings.
Miller steps into the chief job with a long paper trail of loyalty and a record of pushing hard on deportation and agency coordination. Wiles leaves with credit for steadying the building and a new berth on the political side. The president’s public message treated both as assets, not liabilities.
Additional pressure on figures around the Millers has surfaced before, including a sustained harassment campaign that produced federal charges in Massachusetts. Those episodes sit outside the staff change itself but show the temperature around the same circle.
Trump’s announcement keeps the focus on continuity of mission even as the cast rotates. A midterm loss of this size invites second-guessing; the White House answer is a deputy already steeped in the policy fights who now runs the staff.
Further FBI leadership churn under the same administration, such as deputy-level resignations, underscores how personnel moves often follow political shocks. The chief-of-staff post is simply the highest-profile example this week.
Voters handed Republicans a clear midterm rebuke. Trump responded by elevating an adviser who has spent nearly a decade enforcing the same border, trade, and fraud priorities, while keeping his former chief inside the political operation. The next fight will be in Congress; the staff box score already shows who is expected to lead it.

As Chief of Staff, Stephen Miller Will Reinforce Trump's Worst Instincts
His elevation does not bode well for anyone who hoped that Trump would moderate the policies that alienated voters in the midterm elections.
President Donald Trump today announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. That change does not bode well for anyone who hoped that Trump, chastened by his party's disastrous performance in the midterm elections, would moderate the policies that alienated voters.
Miller, previously a deputy chief of staff, is the main architect of Trump's immigration crackdown, which has targeted many peaceful and productive U.S. residents, contrary to the promise that it would focus on "the worst of the worst." Although Trump has intermittently expressed qualms about the impact of immigration enforcement on businesses and their longtime employees, Miller has made it clear that he favors an indiscriminate approach.
A January 2026 profile of Miller in The Atlantic described an exchange that epitomizes his attitude toward immigration. "Stephen, if you had it your way, everyone would look exactly like you," Trump reportedly told Miller, who was arguing about immigration policy with another White House aide. "That's correct," Miller replied.
Since illegal immigration is an "invasion," Miller told reporters in May 2025, the Trump administration was "actively looking" at suspending the writ of habeas corpus to facilitate its mass deportation campaign. "A lot of it depends on whether the courts do the right thing or not," he said. It turned out that Miller was not just spitballing: The New York Times later reported that his comment reflected a serious internal debate about whether to unilaterally override the ancient principle that people nabbed by the government have a right to challenge their detention in court.
Miller's support for aggressive immigration enforcement extends to violence against Americans who object to it. After immigration agents fatally shot Minneapolis protester Alex Pretti in January, Miller defied the video evidence by condemning him as "a domestic terrorist" and "would-be assassin" who "tried to murder federal law enforcement."
Last April, Miller described birthright citizenship as "the gravest and most preposterous of all constitutional abominations." Two months later, after the Supreme Court rejected Trump's attempt to rewrite the 14th Amendment, Miller called it "one of the most destructive and outrageous decisions" in the Court's history.
Miller also was appalled by judicial pushback against Trump's "emergency" tariffs. After the U.S. Court of International Trade rejected them in May 2025, he implied that it had no legitimate role in determining whether the president had the authority he claimed. "The judicial coup is out of control," he wrote on X. Last February, when the Supreme Court agreed that Trump's tariffs were illegal, Miller condemned the decision as "cowardly" and "horrendous," saying the justices were "torturing" the law and the Constitution.
Miller's hostility toward judicial review mirrors Trump's attitude. Also like Trump, Miller has no compunctions about punishing people for constitutionally protected speech.
In November 2023, after Media Matters for America reported that X was "placing ads for Apple, Bravo, IBM, Oracle, and Xfinity next to pro-Nazi content," Miller urged "conservative state Attorneys General" to investigate the organization for "fraud." Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey took Miller's advice, launching investigations that were ultimately blocked by federal courts on First Amendment grounds.
After conservative activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated in September 2025, Miller blamed a "vast domestic terror movement," including "messaging designed to trigger [and] incite violence"—i.e., harsh political rhetoric. "In Charlie's name," he said, "we are going to use every resource we have at the Department of Justice, Homeland Security, and throughout this government to identify, disrupt, dismantle, and destroy these networks."
Miller, in short, is apt to be the opposite of a calming influence on Trump. His elevation seems likely to reinforce the president's worst instincts.

sources.news_title: Trump Replaces Susie Wiles With Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff After GOP Midterm Defeat
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP)—President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, jumping on board during his long shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff.
Miller is a former aide to hard-liner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who served as Trump’s first attorney general.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events said, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
Wiles also released a social media statement Friday.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Wiles Brought Order to Trump’s Campaign
The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
Wiles Showed Unusual Candor in an Interview
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who in turn disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” although she did not deny making the comments that were attributed to her.
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”
Trump ground through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.
Wiles Overcomes Personal Health Struggle
After Wiles revealed she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer, she juggled surgery and treatments alongside her demanding job.
Six months later, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. On social media, she thanked her family, friends, doctors and “everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way” and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support.”
“She’s tough,” Trump said of his chief of staff at a White House event in October. “She’s a tremendous fighter.”
In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer, because she wasn’t due for one for several more months. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.
“Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July,” Wiles told the outlet. “We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist.”
Wiles Is a Seasoned Political Operative
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis’ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.
Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, also worked in the offices of former Jacksonville mayors John Delaney and John Peyton. Her first White House job was as a scheduler for President Ronald Reagan.
In addition to her government and campaign positions, Wiles has worked as a lobbyist. She was a partner at Florida-based Ballard Partners, which rose to prominence in Washington during Trump’s time in the White House. Her varying list of clients included General Motors, a trade group for children’s hospitals, homebuilders, and the city of Jacksonville.
She was also registered as a lobbyist for the Venezuelan television network Globovisión, which was owned by businessperson Raúl Gorrín, who was charged in Miami with money laundering. The firm later called its work for Gorrín a mistake and said Wiles had almost no role in managing the relationship with Gorrín.

AP writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report.

Former Chief of Staff Susie Wiles will move to the “Trump Political Operation,” the president announced in an afternoon post on his Truth Social platform.

The president told reporters outside the White House that he wants Miller to “just run things well.”
“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it, very good politically, and he’s a very good manager. He’ll do a great job,” he said.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries slammed the move, writing on X Friday that Miller “is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands.”
“His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today,” Jeffries, who is poised to become House speaker in January, wrote on X.
Blue wave
The move comes after voters rebuked Trump Tuesday, giving Democrats sizable majorities in both the House and Senate this coming Congress. In a backlash to Trump, Hispanics who voted for the president in 2024 shunned him in the midterms.
Every voter demographic sharply swung toward Democrats, but Latinos shifted sharply, by 21 points, according to an analysis by NPR, and a separate analysis by The Associated Press.
Miller has been a proponent of the Trump administration’s campaign against birthright citizenship, which it lost in a major case at the U.S. Supreme Court.

So you see consistent high rates of welfare use, consistent high rates of criminal activity, consistent failures to assimilate.”
The claim that immigrants commit more crimes than other demographics in the United States is unfounded, according to several studies of national crime statistics compiled by the Migration Policy Institute. The institute found that immigrants in the U.S. commit crimes at lower rates than the U.S.-born population.
The New York Times, reporting those comments by Miller, said that studies have documented the upward mobility of immigrant children and that experts questioned his underlying arguments.

During that same interview, Miller blamed immigrants in the United States for low test scores and healthcare costs, among other issues.
2026 deadly surge
Miller also advocated for the surge of immigration agents into mostly Democrat-led American cities throughout 2026, and did not back down after extreme instances of violence.
In January after federal agents fatally shot Alex Pretti in Minnesota, Miller reposted a video of the killing posted by the Democratic National Committee on X with the comments: “A would-be assassin tried to murder federal law enforcement and the official Democrat account sides with the terrorists.”
Miller steered immigration policies during Trump’s first term.
He has been a fixture of Trump’s political apparatus for a decade, and played a role in Trump’s successful presidential campaign beginning in 2015.

sources.news_title: Stephen Miller, architect of Trump’s immigration policies, replaces Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.
The staff shuffle signals that Trump, now staring down a combative Congress that will soon be controlled by Democrats, is resisting a conciliatory approach after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. Miller is a dogged defender of Trump and his “America First” principles, and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president’s executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events said, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles in a Truth Social post and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Miller is a longtime Trump aide
During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoted unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.
He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.
Miller was a veteran Senate aide who worked for former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., before he joined Trump’s nascent presidential campaign in 2016. Sessions was the first senator to endorse Trump in his first run and later served as his attorney general.
But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely allied with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.
“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”
In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”
Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign
The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
Wiles showed unusual candor in an interview
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”
Trump went through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.
Wiles overcomes personal health struggle
Six months after her diagnosis, Wiles revealed she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. She thanked her family, friends, doctors, and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support” in a statement.
“She’s tough,” Trump said at a White House event in October. “She’s a tremendous fighter.”
In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.
“Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July,” Wiles told the outlet. “We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist.”
Wiles is a seasoned political operative
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ' successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.
Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, also worked in the offices of former Jacksonville mayors John Delaney and John Peyton. Her first White House job was as a scheduler for President Ronald Reagan.
In addition to her government and campaign positions, Wiles has worked as a lobbyist. She was a partner at Florida-based Ballard Partners, which rose to prominence in Washington during Trump’s time in the White House. Her clients included General Motors, a trade group for children’s hospitals, homebuilders, and the city of Jacksonville.
She was also registered as a lobbyist for the Venezuelan television network Globovisión, which was owned by businessperson Raúl Gorrín, who was charged in Miami with money laundering. The firm later called its work for Gorrín a mistake and said Wiles had almost no role in managing the relationship with Gorrín.
