Miller is a dogged defender of Trump and his “America First” principles, and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president’s executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events said, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles in a Truth Social post and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Miller is a longtime Trump aide
During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoted unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.
He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.
Miller was a veteran Senate aide who worked for former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., before he joined Trump’s nascent presidential campaign in 2016. Sessions was the first senator to endorse Trump in his first run and later served as his attorney general.
But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely allied with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.
“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”
In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”
Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign
The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
Wiles showed unusual candor in an interview
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”
Trump went through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.
Wiles overcomes personal health struggle
Six months after her diagnosis, Wiles revealed she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. She thanked her family, friends, doctors, and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support” in a statement.
“She’s tough,” Trump said at a White House event in October. “She’s a tremendous fighter.”
In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.
“Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July,” Wiles told the outlet. “We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist.”
Wiles is a seasoned political operative
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.
Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, also worked in the offices of former Jacksonville mayors John Delaney and John Peyton. Her first White House job was as a scheduler for President Ronald Reagan.
In addition to her government and campaign positions, Wiles has worked as a lobbyist. She was a partner at Florida-based Ballard Partners, which rose to prominence in Washington during Trump’s time in the White House. Her clients included General Motors, a trade group for children’s hospitals, homebuilders, and the city of Jacksonville.
She was also registered as a lobbyist for the Venezuelan television network Globovisión, which was owned by businessperson Raúl Gorrín, who was charged in Miami with money laundering. The firm later called its work for Gorrín a mistake and said Wiles had almost no role in managing the relationship with Gorrín.

sources.text:
Talk about a weave. Donald Trump’s reactions to his party’s midterm-election disaster have been all over the place. He signaled right away that he accepted the terrible results (a first for this sore loser) and even mumbled about working with the Democrats who will now control Congress in January. Yet he deflected blame for the debacle everywhere other than to the man he sees in the gilded mirrors of the White House every day. Would he drift toward retirement quietly and somewhat passively, much like George W. Bush, who was similarly rebuked by the electorate in a second midterm election? Or resort even more to wild theories of unlimited executive power to get his way without any significant involvement from Congress?
We didn’t have to wait long for the answer. Trump has now taken the step that best explains his take on the midterms and where he intends to lead his party and the country, announcing on Truth Social that Stephen Miller is his new White House chief of staff:
I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job! President DONALD J. TRUMP
Blaming Susie Wiles for the midterms isn’t totally surprising since she was part and parcel of the 2024 Trump campaign team that moved into the White House and oversaw the midterm effort, to the limited extent that they were able to do anything other than following the boss’s orders. But putting Miller into her place is a pretty clear signal of defiance to Democrats, to Republicans who wanted a change of direction, and to the electorate.
For one thing, Miller has overseen policy for the White House with an extremely broad portfolio that extends beyond his signature obsession with immigration. As The Atlantic explained earlier this year, he has placed his distinctive stamp of rigid ideological fidelity across the full range of controversial issues:
Steve Bannon, a former Trump adviser and a Miller ally, describes him as Trump’s “prime minister.” Miller has a role in nearly every area about which he cares deeply: immigration and border security, yes, but also national security, foreign policy, trade, military action, and policing. He may draft a flurry of executive orders one day, lead a meeting on lowering domestic beef prices the next, and travel to deliver a fiery speech of his own — think Trump at his angriest and most dystopian, without any of the president’s impish humor — the following week.
Yes, dating back to the reputation he earned as a nativist crank while working for Jeff Sessions in the pre-Trump Senate, Miller is especially devoted to the task of mass deportation of undocumented immigrants and, beyond that, to eliminating to the maximum extent possible avenues for legal immigration, too. He has famously lashed subordinates in all the federal agencies involved in immigration policy to meet tight quotas for deportations, and he clearly has no problems with the enforcement excesses that have made ICE widely regarded as an American gestapo. That Trump is promoting rather than firing Miller shows he doesn’t understand or doesn’t care about the loss of support among Latinos that, more than any other individual factor, fed the midterm debacle. Miller is deeply responsible for losing 2024 Trump voters who supported border control and deportation of violent criminals but never bargained for the terror ICE has inflicted on immigrant communities or the unapologetic racism that underlies Miller’s approach.
And that may be the scariest thing of all about his new base of power: He has two more years to act on his deep belief in the Great Replacement theory. This is the idea that traitorous liberals are deliberately destroying the country through a conspiracy to drown native-born white Americans in a sea of shiftless immigrants who trade illegal votes for welfare benefits and the opportunity to commit crimes. Trump talks about this nightmare scenario all the time as part of his demagogic pitch to the MAGA base. But for Miller, it’s an article of faith.
Some Trump defenders will try to rationalize Miller’s elevation as insignificant, a semi-automatic move up the ladder for the Trump loyalist who was technically Wiles’s deputy. It’s true that he may bring more discipline and fewer leaks to the White House staff. But it will likely be the discipline of sheer fanaticism and intolerance for dissent.
Trump’s big decision in the wake of the midterms is whether to learn something from his party’s setback and seek to wind down his final term in office in a dignified manner or instead try to implement the worst and most divisive elements of his agenda come hell or high water. There’s little question Miller would take the administration down this second path, and his promotion will give him that chance.

President Donald Trump announced on Friday, November 6, that his longtime adviser, Stephen Miller, will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff. The news comes just three days after Republicans suffered devastating and historic losses in the midterm elections, and after weeks of denials from the White House that Wiles was on her way out.
It marks one of the most significant personnel changes of Trump’s second term, removing the first woman ever to hold the position and elevating one of his most controversial figures, even as voters appeared to reject the president’s hardline positions in Tuesday’s elections. Miller, a controversial figure and a leading architect of President Trump’s immigration policies, has worked closely with the president since his 2016 campaign.
While the president has repeatedly denied reports that he was considering replacing Wiles, the news follows reports that senior administration figures have spent weeks positioning themselves as replacements. Some accounts also indicated that Wiles may have resigned yesterday.
What Trump Said – and the Future for Wiles
“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
The president added that Wiles would not leave his orbit entirely and would instead take on a new role in his political operation.
“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her services as Chief of Staff — she has done a great job!” he continued.
This comes after reports this week that President Trump is preparing to keep raising money for his MAGA Inc. super PAC, intending to influence Republican races in the future—potentially including the 2028 presidential election. Given Wiles’ success in directing his 2024 presidential campaign, Wiles may now be used to drum up support for President Trump’s political efforts and help establish his long-term legacy. But with Republicans sorely disappointed with his performance and the state of the Iran war, Wiles could face a major challenge.
What Wiles Said
In her own statement, Wiles confirmed that she was leaving her post. She thanked the Trump administration and touted its successes so far.
“Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff,” she wrote. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”
More than anything, Wiles said, she was grateful for the “extraordinary people” she worked alongside.
“While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will,” she added.
The two statements don’t immediately suggest any bad blood between Wiles and the president. However, in recent weeks, reports have frequently indicated that, behind the scenes, the president has been asking about Wiles’ performance and has even expressed concern about allegations that she used her influence to benefit her daughter’s career, Katie Wiles, and other Trump advisers working with her.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio was complimentary in his own statement, writing on X that Wiles “served our country with exceptional strength, devotion, and grace.”
“She has done an incredible job serving our country and President Trump,” he also said, adding that he was grateful for her service and friendship.
A Wartime Consigliere?
The decision might offer insight into how Trump sees the remainder of his time as president, with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress and the war with Iran still not over.
In June 2023, NPR reported that Trump had long seemed to be searching for a “wartime consigliere”—someone resembling his former lawyer Roy Cohn, known for his confrontational approach to defending the president’s interests. That kind of talk has returned after the announcement that Wiles will step down as chief of staff.
Miller has been described similarly. In March 2026, The American Prospect called him Trump’s “wartime consigliere,” citing his aggressive efforts to defend the president’s immigration agenda. Miller’s appointment suggests the president is now prioritizing confrontation over everything else. Trump talks about making deals with Democrats in Congress, but with Miller in charge, he’ll have a fierce proponent of his agenda directing his staff for, presumably, the next two years.
National Security Journal editor-in-chief Harry Kazianis said on November 6 that a long-time Trump White House staffer confirmed that mindset to him.
“Trump wanted a wartime consigliere. He gets that in Stephen Miller. The problem is that Miller never wants a truce or peace,” the source said.

Donald Trump has announced that Stephen Miller, his senior adviser and current deputy chief of staff, will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump said Wiles, whom he praised for doing an “outstanding job,” would move to the Trump Political Operation. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!” he added.
The unexpected announcement came Friday afternoon, only days after Democrats scored a sweeping election victory that delivered a major setback to Trump and congressional Republicans.
The scale of the Democratic win was so significant that Republicans could remain shut out of the congressional majority for much of the next decade—an alarming prospect for conservatives who had urged Trump to overhaul his team.
Asked about the change Friday, Trump told reporters that he had decided “to make a change.” He described Wiles as having done a “very good job” and added: “We gotta make moves. Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”
That explanation differed from the account offered by a senior White House official, who told Our News Outlet that Wiles had “gave her resignation last night.”
The conflicting descriptions have fueled questions about whether Trump initiated the transition or whether Wiles chose to leave, despite the president’s public assertion that a change was necessary.
Donald Trump has fired his White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and replaced her with his top adviser Stephen Miller
Wiles said serving in the White House was an honor in a brief statement issued after Trump announced the change on Truth Social
Wiles was the first woman in US history to serve as White House chief of staff
Trump said Miller had “been with me from the beginning,” describing him as “very good politically” and predicting that he “will do a great job.”
Wiles shared her farewell message on X shortly after Trump made his announcement.
“Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff,” she wrote Friday. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime.”
“I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First. More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside.”
Her exit follows a report by Our News Outlet in June that she was preparing to leave the position after the midterm elections.
Although Wiles rejected that report at the time, she departed only days after the election results were announced.

White House chief of staff replaced by Stephen Miller
US President Donald Trump has replaced chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, elevating the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies to run the White House after Republicans lost control of Congress in this week's midterm elections.
The shake-up on Friday puts a longtime Trump loyalist and firebrand policy adviser in charge of steering Trump's agenda as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate, and an expected wave of congressional investigations.
White House officials told Reuters that Miller's selection suggests Trump will take an aggressive approach to domestic policy and politics.
Miller is a veteran of Trump's first term in office in 2017-2021. Since Trump's return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially been deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he wielded outsize influence across much of Trump's domestic agenda and has had the ear of the president.
He is perhaps best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a target of 3000 arrests a day. In pursuit of that target, federal immigration agents expanded their list of targets to include migrants who had been living in the United States for decades.
In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisers," and he praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job." He said the change would take effect on Monday.
Wiles, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump's political operation, according to a White House official.
Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday's election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows.
This week, he said the White House needed to be "more aggressive" as Democrats retake congressional power, according to a person briefed on the matter.
Wiles' allies in the White House began sharing concerns with others on Wednesday about her potential replacement, the person said.
"He's rewarding those most loyal to him. He's not changing course," said another White House official.

Three days after Republicans suffered a political shellacking in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump has made one of the biggest personnel changes of his second administration.
Susie Wiles is out.
Stephen Miller is in.
And anyone expecting the White House to respond to Tuesday’s election results by suddenly going soft might want to reconsider.
Trump announced Friday afternoon that Miller, his longtime adviser and deputy chief of staff, will take over as White House chief of staff on Monday, November 9.
The president made the announcement on Truth Social, writing:

Trump also explained what will happen to Wiles.

Republicans have just lost control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats are preparing to take over Capitol Hill, launch investigations and challenge Trump’s agenda during the final two years of his presidency.
And Trump has responded by putting Stephen Miller in charge of the West Wing.
Not exactly the personnel choice of a president preparing to wave the white flag.
Miller has been part of Trump’s inner political circle since the 2016 presidential campaign. He helped shape some of the administration’s most consequential immigration policies and has become one of its most recognizable defenders.
He has been central to Trump’s border-security and deportation agenda, advocating aggressive enforcement and a tougher approach to illegal immigration.
To his supporters, Miller is a disciplined, determined policy strategist who knows exactly what the president wants.
To his critics, he represents some of the administration’s most controversial priorities.
Either way, nobody in Washington is going to mistake Stephen Miller for a caretaker chief of staff.
Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff.
Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.
More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.
— Susie Wiles (@SusieWiles47) November 6, 2026
The White House hasn’t described the appointment as a strategic shift, and Trump offered no detailed explanation for the timing.
But Miller’s elevation puts one of the administration’s most combative policy advisers in charge of coordinating the president’s staff and helping manage the daily machinery of the White House.
That’s a very different responsibility from serving as a senior policy adviser.
The chief of staff decides who gets access to the president, helps establish priorities, coordinates senior officials and attempts to keep the entire operation moving in the same direction.
It’s a position that can make or break an administration.
And Stephen Miller is about to discover that running the White House involves considerably more than writing tough immigration policy.
There’s Congress to manage.
Cabinet secretaries to coordinate.
Political crises to navigate.
And, beginning in January, a Democratic majority that will be considerably less interested in helping Trump accomplish anything.
In other words, welcome to the job.
Meanwhile, Wiles’ departure marks the end of a remarkable chapter in Trump’s political career.
The veteran Florida Republican strategist helped guide Trump’s successful 2024 presidential campaign and became the first woman in American history to serve as White House chief of staff.
She was widely credited with bringing structure and discipline to a political operation that had often been criticized for its internal turmoil.
That was no small accomplishment.
During Trump’s first administration, the position became something of a revolving door.
Reince Priebus, John Kelly, Mick Mulvaney and Mark Meadows all held the job.
Wiles, by contrast, remained at Trump’s side throughout the first 22 months of his second term, making her his longest-serving White House chief of staff.
She also earned a reputation for operating behind the scenes rather than competing for television time.
But her tenure was hardly without controversy.
In December 2025, Vanity Fair published candid comments attributed to Wiles about Trump and several senior administration figures, generating headlines and questions about internal White House relationships.
Wiles subsequently remained in her position.
Then came a personal challenge.
In March, she revealed that she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer. She continued working during treatment and announced in September that she was cancer-free.
Friday’s announcement did not attribute her departure to her health.
Instead, Trump said she would move into his political organization, an indication that he intends to keep her experience and campaign expertise within his orbit.
Wiles confirmed the change in her own statement.
“Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff. Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” she wrote.
She said she was proud of the administration’s accomplishments, including its work on border security, taxes and the economy.
And she made clear that leaving the White House would not mean abandoning Trump.
“While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”
That doesn’t sound like somebody preparing to join the Lincoln Project.
It sounds like a veteran political operative moving from the West Wing to the political battlefield.
And that battlefield is about to get very crowded.
The Democratic victories Tuesday have completely changed the political environment in which Trump must operate.
Instead of working with Republican majorities in Congress, the administration will face hostile committee chairmen, aggressive oversight and lawmakers eager to examine virtually every major decision of his presidency.
Everything from immigration enforcement and government spending to foreign policy could become the subject of congressional investigations.
There will be subpoenas.
There will be hearings.
There will be demands for documents.
And if recent Washington history is any guide, there will be more television cameras than anyone knows what to do with.
Miller will be responsible for helping the administration navigate all of it.
Some Democrats will undoubtedly see his promotion as further evidence that Trump has no intention of moderating his agenda after the election losses.
Republican supporters of the president may see precisely the opposite: a signal that Trump is bringing one of his most committed advisers into the top management position at the moment he needs someone prepared for a fight.
Former Trump chief of staff Mark Meadows offered his own assessment of Miller’s strengths Friday, describing him as thoughtful, organized and focused on making sure decisions are carried out.
That’s a side of Miller the public may not see as often as his televised clashes with political opponents.
But organization and execution will matter enormously in the months ahead.
After all, it’s one thing to promise a tough response to illegal immigration.
It’s another to make sure the Department of Homeland Security, Justice Department, White House legal team and congressional operation are all moving in the same direction while Democrats demand answers.
And that’s just one issue.
The administration also faces continuing disputes over the economy, spending, the war with Iran and the political consequences of the midterms.
Trump has spent much of his political career relying on trusted advisers who understand his priorities without requiring a lengthy explanation.
Miller certainly fits that description.
But the choice also concentrates enormous responsibility in the hands of a man whose strongest public reputation is as an ideological and policy advocate.
Now he’ll be expected to manage people, priorities and political problems across the entire White House.
And the stakes could hardly be higher.
For Wiles, Friday closes a historic tenure and opens another role in Trump’s political operation.
For Miller, it represents the biggest promotion of his Washington career.
For Trump, it’s his first major personnel response to a midterm defeat that has dramatically changed the balance of power.
And for Democrats preparing to take control of Congress?
Well, they were probably hoping Tuesday’s victory would put Trump on the defensive.
Instead, the president just handed the keys to the West Wing to Stephen Miller.
Love him or hate him, that’s not a man known for backing away from a fight.
Washington’s next two years were already shaping up to be contentious.
Trump may have just turned up the thermostat.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, jumping on board during his long shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff.
Miller is a former aide to hard-liner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who served as Trump’s first attorney general.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events said, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.” alt=”” />
Wiles also released a social media statement Friday.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign
The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
Wiles showed unusual candor in an interview
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who in turn disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” although she did not deny making the comments that were attributed to her.” alt=”” />
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”
Trump ground through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.” alt=”” />
Wiles overcomes personal health struggle
After Wiles revealed she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer, she juggled surgery and treatments alongside her demanding job.
Six months later, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. On social media, she thanked her family, friends, doctors and “everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way” and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support.”
“She’s tough,” Trump said of his chief of staff at a White House event in October. “She’s a tremendous fighter.”” alt=”” />
In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer, because she wasn’t due for one for several more months. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.
“Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July,” Wiles told the outlet. “We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist.”” alt=”” />
Wiles is a seasoned political operative
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.
Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, also worked in the offices of former Jacksonville mayors John Delaney and John Peyton. Her first White House job was as a scheduler for President Ronald Reagan.
In addition to her government and campaign positions, Wiles has worked as a lobbyist. She was a partner at Florida-based Ballard Partners, which rose to prominence in Washington during Trump’s time in the White House. Her varying list of clients included General Motors, a trade group for children’s hospitals, homebuilders, and the city of Jacksonville.
She was also registered as a lobbyist for the Venezuelan television network Globovisión, which was owned by businessperson Raúl Gorrín, who was charged in Miami with money laundering. The firm later called its work for Gorrín a mistake and said Wiles had almost no role in managing the relationship with Gorrín.

President Donald Trump announced that Stephen Miller, currently Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy, will become White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. More than anything, I'm grateful for the extraordinary people I've had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."
The announcement comes just days after the 2026 midterm elections, in which Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate, along with dozens of governorships and state legislatures, according to The Independent. That outlet described the timing as Trump "axing" Wiles in the wake of a resounding defeat. CNN Politics confirmed the replacement roughly 17 minutes after POLITICO's report, identifying Miller as a longtime aide to the president.
Miller, 41, has spent much of the last two years implementing the administration's mass deportation campaign, per The Independent, which also noted his advocacy for policies restricting immigration from non-white-majority countries and for using federal funds to penalize jurisdictions led by Democrats. The Independent's characterization of those policies as "harsh" is that outlet's framing; the underlying actions — border enforcement, deportation operations, and federal funding conditions — are matters of public record.
Social media reaction was immediate. X account @TrumpDailyPosts posted: "BREAKING: President Trump just added wartime Consigliere Stephen Miller as new Chief of Staff and Susie Wiles out. Things just got very interesting." The post, which included a link, framed the move in combative terms; it is a social-media post, not a report.
Wiles was widely described by other outlets as the administration's "rudder," credited with keeping the president's agenda on track and running a smooth operation in contrast to the first Trump term. Rumors of her departure had been dismissed by the president and top aides before Friday's announcement, according to one outlet's coverage.

This is a war-footing move, and it's about time. Susie Wiles ran a tight ship, and she deserves credit for steering the agenda through two years of nonstop incoming. But the midterms were a shellacking, and when the voters send a message that loud, the president needs a fighter at the helm — not a manager. Stephen Miller is that fighter.

The same people who called border enforcement radical are the ones who watched the 2026 map turn blue and want to pretend the lesson is "moderate harder." Patriots know better. The base didn't stay home because Trump was too tough on the border — they stayed home because Washington didn't deliver enough of the fight they voted for.
Miller in the chief-of-staff chair means the deportation machine doesn't slow down, the funding fights with sanctuary cities don't get softer, and the West Wing stops worrying about what the legacy media thinks. With a hostile Congress, the president's pen and his agencies become the whole ballgame. Who better to run that than the man who wrote the playbook?
The question now: will Republicans in Congress get behind the president's agenda, or will they spend the next two years auditioning for the media's approval while America First stalls? Miller's promotion puts the choice in plain sight. Patriots should be watching — and calling their representatives.

Trump replaces Susie Wiles as chief of staff with Stephen Miller
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies.
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, jumping on board during his long shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff.
Miller is a former aide to hard-liner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who served as Trump’s first attorney general.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events said, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
Wiles also released a social media statement Friday.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign
The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
Wiles showed unusual candor in an interview
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who in turn disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” although she did not deny making the comments that were attributed to her.
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”
Trump ground through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.
Wiles overcomes personal health struggle
After Wiles revealed she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer, she juggled surgery and treatments alongside her demanding job.
Six months later, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. On social media, she thanked her family, friends, doctors and “everyone who prayed for me, checked in, and supported me along the way” and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support.”
“She’s tough,” Trump said of his chief of staff at a White House event in October. “She’s a tremendous fighter.”
In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer, because she wasn’t due for one for several more months. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.
“Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July,” Wiles told the outlet. “We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist.”
Wiles is a seasoned political operative
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ‘ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.
Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, also worked in the offices of former Jacksonville mayors John Delaney and John Peyton. Her first White House job was as a scheduler for President Ronald Reagan.
In addition to her government and campaign positions, Wiles has worked as a lobbyist. She was a partner at Florida-based Ballard Partners, which rose to prominence in Washington during Trump’s time in the White House. Her varying list of clients included General Motors, a trade group for children’s hospitals, homebuilders, and the city of Jacksonville.
She was also registered as a lobbyist for the Venezuelan television network Globovisión, which was owned by businessperson Raúl Gorrín, who was charged in Miami with money laundering. The firm later called its work for Gorrín a mistake and said Wiles had almost no role in managing the relationship with Gorrín.
AP writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report.

Trump taps Stephen Miller as new White House chief of staff
Susie Wiles is leaving as White House chief of staff after sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections and will be replaced by Stephen Miller, the powerful domestic policy adviser who has helped drive the administration’s immigration crackdown, President Donald Trump announced today.
Wiles’ departure and the ascent of Miller will fundamentally shift the circle of advisers around Trump as the White House absorbs the shock of the midterm elections.
Wiles, the first woman to hold the top staff job in the West Wing, helped steer Trump to his election victory in 2024, playing a central role in his return to power four years after his loss to Joe Biden.
She is the highest-ranking White House official to leave in the wake of the midterm elections, which resulted in the loss of Republican majorities in the House and Senate and served as a rebuke of Trump’s handling of the economy and the war with Iran.
The Republican wipeout has inflamed tensions within the administration, as officials brace for congressional investigations by Democrats and further turnover in the West Wing and the Cabinet.
Wiles came into the job having established a rapport with Trump and a level of trust that none of his four first-term chiefs of staff had enjoyed.

Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Unlike some of Trump’s previous chiefs of staff, Wiles made clear she did not consider her job as trying to fundamentally change the president. But she tried to influence his decisions on core issues including his immigration crackdown, even if only on the margins, according to people with knowledge of her role. She pushed for the appointments of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and both have been seen by many outside the government as stabilizing figures.
During Wiles’ tenure, the president pushed the boundaries of executive power, using the levers of his government to punish his enemies, challenge the courts and target journalists.
Since Trump’s decision in February to take the United States to war with Iran, the administration has struggled to respond to the conflict’s economic and political effects, including spiking fuel prices.
Trump has publicly expressed his confidence in Wiles in recent months. But behind the scenes, there were signs that her standing with the president was shaky, according to officials with knowledge of the dynamics.
Trump began cutting Wiles out of hiring decisions, including when he chose an inexperienced television pundit to replace press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
And Trump began to criticize his chief of staff in front of other staff members, including over decisions he had approved, according to people familiar with his remarks.
After the elections, Trump made it clear to some advisers that he was unhappy with Wiles and his political team, who persuaded him to sign off on his super political action committee spending $400 million to help Republicans in the midterms. The president had been reluctant to approve the spending and agreed to it only in September.
To Wiles’ supporters, the criticism of her was an effort to assign blame for a political strategy largely driven by Trump. They blamed her detractors inside and outside the administration for spreading information meant to undercut her with Trump, including stories about her daughter’s lobbying work.
Wiles was diagnosed with breast cancer in early 2026. She stayed in her role as she started treatment and recently announced that she was cancer-free.

Mr Miller starts his new job on Monday.

The US president made the announcement on Friday, local time, in a social media post.

In reality, the switch sidelines one of his most senior staff members, whom he said as recently as last month had "zero chance" of replacing.
"I want to thank her for her service as chief of staff," Mr Trump's post read. "She has done a great job!"
Later, Mr Trump told reporters at the White House he "wanted to make a change".

In March, Ms Wiles announced she would be taking time away from her role after being diagnosed with breast cancer.

Before that, Mr Miller worked for Senator Jeff Sessions, who was renowned as one of the chamber's loudest and most uncompromising voices on the subject.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year.
Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.
The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday’s midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target. Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president’s executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told the Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.
Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.
“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement.
The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.
Miller is tied to immigration policies that voters said went too far
During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoting unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.
He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.
He joined Trump on Friday for his trip to Florida, and the president noted to reporters that “Stephen has been with me from the beginning.
“He gets it; very good politically,” Trump said as he departed the White House. “He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”
But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely associated with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.
“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”
In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”
Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign
Trump on Friday praised Wiles, the veteran Florida operative who joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid, as having done a “very good job, great job.”
But he added, “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”
Wiles, 69, is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.
She has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.
Wiles stuck with the job even after her breast cancer diagnosis. Deep into the midterm campaign, six months after having revealed her diagnosis, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear.
In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.
Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ' successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.
Wiles once said Trump had ‘an alcoholic’s personality’
But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”
Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.
In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”
“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”
___
Associated Press writers Michelle L. Price in Washington and Jill Colvin in New York contributed to this report.

Trump sacks Susie Wiles after midterm rout, picks Stephen Miller as chief of staff
Miller has been a central figure in Trump's political circle since the President's first campaign for the White House in 2016, when he joined as a speechwriter. Over the years, he has emerged as one of the most influential voices in Trump's inner circle, particularly on immigration and national security.
US President Donald Trump has replaced White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with his longtime aide Stephen Miller, days after Republicans suffered a sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump announced the decision on his social media platform Truth Social on Friday, praising Wiles for her work in the administration and confirming that Miller would take over the influential position.
Wiles, who became the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will continue working with Trump's political organisation, the President said. Her departure comes just days after Democrats secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, delivering a major setback to Trump's Republican Party midway through his second term.
Miller, currently serving as White House deputy chief of staff, is among Trump's closest and longest-serving advisers. He has played a central role in shaping the administration's immigration agenda and is widely regarded as one of the key architects of Trump's hardline policies on border security and deportations.
REPUBLICANS SUFFER SWEEPING MIDTERM DEFEAT
The leadership change comes in the aftermath of the November 3 midterm elections, in which Democrats made significant gains across the country, flipping Republican-held seats and ending the party's control of both chambers of Congress.
The results marked a sharp political setback for Trump, whose party had entered the elections with narrow majorities in the House and Senate. Democrats capitalised on voter dissatisfaction with the administration, particularly over the rising cost of living, the economic impact of tariffs and the unpopular US war with Iran.
Several traditionally Republican-leaning states also witnessed significant swings towards Democrats. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator in nearly a century, while Democrats defeated Trump's hand-picked Senate candidate in South Carolina, a state the President had won comfortably in the 2024 presidential election.
The losses are expected to complicate Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency, with Democrats set to gain control of congressional committees and greater powers to investigate his administration.
WHO ARE STEPHEN MILLER AND SUSIE WILES?
Miller has been a central figure in Trump's political circle since the President's first campaign for the White House in 2016, when he joined as a speechwriter. Over the years, he has emerged as one of the most influential voices in Trump's inner circle, particularly on immigration and national security.
Wiles, meanwhile, was widely credited with bringing discipline and organisational control to Trump's political operations. She joined his team during the 2016 presidential campaign, managed his Florida campaign in 2020 and oversaw his nationwide campaign in 2024.
She was appointed White House chief of staff at the beginning of Trump's second term and became his longest-serving chief of staff. Trump had gone through four people in the position during his first presidency.
Her exit also comes months after she publicly disclosed an early-stage breast cancer diagnosis in March 2026. Following surgery and treatment, she announced in September that she no longer showed evidence of the disease.
Wiles said in a statement following Trump's announcement that serving in the White House had been the honour of a lifetime and reaffirmed her commitment to the President and his political mission.
DOJ SEES FRESH EXODUS AS TWO TOP OFFICIALS RESIGN AFTER MIDTERM DEFEAT
Two senior officials at the US Department of Justice resigned on Friday, adding to a growing wave of departures from the department following the Republican Party's defeat in the midterm elections, which handed control of both chambers of Congress to Democrats.
John Eisenberg, who headed the Justice Department's National Security Division, and Jason Reding Quiones, the former US attorney for the Southern District of Florida, stepped down a day after Harmeet Dhillon resigned as chief of the department's civil rights division.
Their exits leave the Justice Department without leaders for two major initiatives pursued by the Trump administration — revisiting earlier investigations involving the President and taking action against higher education institutions.
The reasons behind the latest resignations were not immediately clear. However, senior government officials frequently leave their positions after midterm elections, particularly when the ruling party suffers significant losses. With Democrats preparing to launch investigations into Trump's administration and business dealings, the departures come at a politically sensitive time for the department.
QUIONES WAS CENTRAL TO INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP'S POLITICAL ADVERSARIES
Quiones played a prominent role in the administration's efforts to reopen investigations involving Trump's political opponents and revisit earlier criminal probes concerning the President.
His office examined the investigations into Trump's handling of classified documents after he left office in 2021, as well as alleged contacts between his 2016 presidential campaign and Russia.
The probe sought to establish that Trump had been the target of a prolonged criminal conspiracy. However, it has not led to any criminal charges so far. Joseph diGenova, the prosecutor who had been supervising the investigation, resigned in September.
Quiones' tenure in Miami was also marked by significant staff departures. Dozens of prosecutors left the office, while some who had handled cases against people accused of storming the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, were fired.
His office was also involved in the administration's pressure campaigns against Cuba and Venezuela. It brought criminal charges against former Cuban President Raul Castro and is prosecuting Alex Saab, a Colombian-born businessman with close ties to Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Venezuela deported Saab in May.
EISENBERG'S DIVISION INVOLVED IN CONTROVERSIAL DOJ ACTIONS
Eisenberg maintained a relatively low public profile, but the National Security Division under his leadership was involved in several contentious Justice Department operations.
These included an unusual search of a Washington Post reporter's home as part of an investigation into leaks. The division also helped pursue the deportation of an Afghan lawful permanent resident who had not been charged with any crime, using a secretive court established in 1996 to handle cases involving alleged foreign terrorists.

sources.news_title: NARASIMHAN: The Trump administration is running out of women
sources.text:
What does it take to lose your job in the Trump administration?
Lately, the answer seems to depend more on what you look like than what you have done.
Just today, Trump revealed that Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as the White House Chief of Staff, following the Democrats’ landslide victory in midterm elections. Notably, Wiles was the first woman to ever hold the position.
A few weeks ago, Kimberly Guilfoyle’s forced resignation as ambassador to Greece was announced on live television during the first White House briefing by the new press secretary, Katie Zacharia. Days later, Zacharia herself was fired just five days into the job, following a debut that the BBC described as “disastrous” and sparked a slew of questions about her qualifications.
These departures are just the latest in a broader pattern. Kristi Noem, Pam Bondi, Lori Chavez-DeRemer, and Tulsi Gabbard, four of Trump’s eight female Cabinet-level officials, left within about three months of one another this spring. All of them were replaced by men. In August, Karoline Leavitt resigned as press secretary, ending her tenure as the youngest woman to ever hold the position.
This imbalance is far from a coincidence. Within the Trump administration, women are held to a far higher standard of accountability than their male counterparts, regardless of competence.
Male officials, meanwhile, have faced consistent calls for their resignation with few consequences. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth accidentally disclosed secret war plans in a group chat that included a journalist. FBI Director Kash Patel has faced allegations of excessive drinking and personal use of a government plane. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick appeared in Justice Department files as a visitor to Jeffrey Epstein’s private island. Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. continues to push debunked claims linking vaccines to autism. All of them remain in their posts.
The man who accepted the blame for that leaked group chat, former National Security Advisor Mike Waltz, was simply moved to the UN Ambassador position, a job that had been promised to Trump’s longtime female ally in Congress, Elise Stefanik. Stefanik wound up politically isolated and chose not to run for re-election.
This begs the important question: what did the Cabinet’s women do?
Gabbard notably resigned after facing criticism for her non-endorsement of the decision to strike Iran. Bondi was ousted over the Epstein files and falling short on prosecuting Trump’s enemies. Chavez-DeRemer stepped down amidst an internal investigation regarding complaints of misconduct. Noem was dismissed after a series of Congressional hearings in which she asserted that the president knew about her $220 million self-centering Department of Homeland Security ad campaign. Instead, she became the Special Envoy to the Shield of Americas initiative, a role that expired last month.
Trump was eager to publicize the number of females in his initial second-term cabinet, higher than that of any previous Republican president. Ironically, though, upon returning to office, Trump was quick to sign an executive order gutting Diversity, Equity and Inclusion programs throughout the federal government, placing all federal DEI staff on paid leave. He has consistently argued against DEI programs in the private sector and in universities, insisting that identity should have no bearing on who rises to the top, while simultaneously using his cabinet’s diversity as one of his biggest talking points.
It is impossible to claim a merit-based system when its rewards and punishments fall unevenly.
This fundamental contradiction is critical considering women’s broader role in politics. In the current Congress, women only hold about 28% of seats, representing 42% of Democrats but only 15% of Republicans. At the same time, an informal Her Campus survey in August found that over 80% of young college-educated women are dissatisfied with current political leadership and 75% are concerned about the midterm outcomes.
When the most visible women in politics are first on the chopping block, it actively shapes who aspires to serve, shrinking the pool of female role models and reinforcing the age-old stereotype that women are incapable of holding power. Because we are already deeply underrepresented, even this small decline in leadership could stall progress by years — women have made up just 3.5% of everyone who has ever served in Congress.
Over the last few weeks, Vanderbilt students showed up to the polls. Elections are one of the few moments where we help set the standards our leaders are held to, and with every vote, we have the power to shape the rooms we one day occupy.
Women are not failing at a higher rate than men. They are being held to a stricter standard, and an administration that claims to value only merit cannot condemn misconduct for half of the population and excuse it for everyone else.
Now that the votes are counted, the work does not end. I urge you to ask yourself what kind of leadership you are willing to accept, and who that leadership truly serves. Research, educate yourself, and involve yourself with the political process knowing what is at stake. The next generation of girls certainly does.
